summary.summary: Barnet's borrowing is scaling fast: having historically funded capital spending from internal cash, the council borrowed a further £159.44m in 2025/26, lifting total debt from £1.157bn to £1.317bn, with another £49.36m of existing debt refinanced in-year. Treasury investments fell to £49.875m (from £61.621m) — described as 'broadly at the council's liquidity buffer', the minimum cash its strategy allows — and the report acknowledges managing 'relatively low cash balances' through a volatile rate environment. Outside the treasury book sit £422.731m of non-treasury investments, including loans to council-owned subsidiaries, third-party developers and community organisations, plus gilts held against Brent Cross Plot 1 commercial agreements. Loan-level detail, the CFR and the maturity ladder are in Appendix A, presented with the outturn to Cabinet on 9 June 2026.

signals.headline: £159.44m borrowed in 2025/26, taking total debt from £1.157bn to £1.317bn (+14%), the second year of heavy external borrowing since the internal-funding era ended in 2024/25
signals.why: Barnet has become a large, recurring borrower whose capital programme now depends on continuous access to PWLB and market debt.

signals.headline: Treasury investments of £49.875m at 31 March 2026 were 'broadly at the council's liquidity buffer' — the lowest cash holding its strategy permits — down from £61.621m a year earlier
signals.why: Sitting at the floor means any cash-flow shock converts directly into new short-term borrowing.

signals.headline: £422.731m of non-treasury investments outstanding at 31 March 2026, including loans to local-authority-owned subsidiaries, third-party developers and community organisations
signals.why: A sum equal to a third of the council's debt is lent outside the treasury strategy's safeguards, with repayment resting on developers' and subsidiaries' performance.

news_drafts.headline: Barnet used £45.9m of £55.7m government-approved support in 2025/26 and delivered 95.8% of savings
news_drafts.lead:
Barnet Council used £45.9m of the £55.7m in Exceptional Financial Support (government permission to borrow and sell assets to cover day-to-day spending) approved for 2025/26, about £10m less than allowed, according to papers for its Cabinet on 12 October. The council also delivered 95.8% of its planned savings and stayed within its agreed budget that year.

For 2026/27, the government has approved in principle up to £79.6m, of which £73.6m is expected to be needed. The council is seeking approval for 2027/28 and awaits clarification of the process from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. Its Financial Sustainability Plan says support is likely to remain necessary in 2027/28 and potentially 2028/29. It sets a £200m target for financial benefits by 2029/30, against a forecast budget gap of £198m, with the aim of ending reliance on the support by March 2029. The papers say the plan's savings are not yet in the medium-term financial strategy (the council's five-year financial plan), and will be added once each has a business case, a named owner and delivery milestones.

The support must be repaid, and the borrowing carries yearly costs in interest and minimum revenue provision (the amount set aside each year to pay off past borrowing). These are put at £9.6m in 2027/28, rising to £13.2m, £17.4m and £22.6m in 2030/31, a total of £62.75m, before falling to zero in 2031/32. The council's papers also name social care demand, homelessness and housing benefit rates not updated since 2011 among the main pressures.
news_drafts.paper_title: Annex A - Our Plan for Financial Sustainability 2026-29

news_drafts.headline: Barnet delivered 95.8% of planned savings in 2025/26 and used £10m less government support than approved
news_drafts.lead:
Barnet delivered 95.8% of its planned savings in 2025/26, stayed within its agreed budget and used about £10m less exceptional financial support than government had approved. That support is permission to borrow, or sell assets, to cover day-to-day spending, and is a last resort. The figures are in the council's financial sustainability plan, which goes to its Finance and Growth Overview and Scrutiny Sub-Committee. The same plan says the support "is likely to remain necessary in 2027/28 and potentially 2028/29".

The plan shows recurring savings and income building to £70m by 2027/28, £100m by 2028/29 and £200m by 2029/30. Residual support of £43m is forecast for 2027/28 and £49m for 2028/29, falling to nothing in 2029/30. The council's medium-term financial strategy, its financial plan for the next several years, forecasts a budget gap of £198m by 2029/30 because spending is expected to grow faster than income. The council aims to end its reliance on the support by March 2029. The strategy does not yet include any service savings from the plan. Proposals will be added once they have business cases, named owners and assessed delivery risks.

Borrowing carries a cost. Interest and minimum revenue provision, the amount set aside each year to pay off past borrowing, linked to the support rise from £9.552m in 2027/28 to £22.611m in 2030/31.

news_drafts.headline: Barnet forecasts needing £73.298m in exceptional government support for 2026-27, down £6m on plan
news_drafts.lead:
Barnet Council expects to need £73.298m of exceptional financial support (EFS) from government to balance its 2026-27 budget, £6m less than the £79.298m originally approved. EFS is permission to borrow, or sell assets, to cover day-to-day spending, and is a last resort.

The figures are in a report on the financial outturn (the actual figures for the year just ended, compared with the budget) and 2026-27 budget management, prepared for the Children and Education Overview and Scrutiny Sub-Committee's meeting on 8 October 2026.

The report says the council "remains reliant" on EFS to balance this year's budget. The papers give the reduction in the forecast but, in the material reviewed, no breakdown of what produced it.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C – Savings & Income Generation Proposals
findings.headline: Duke of Edinburgh Accreditation Service closure targeted to remove £192k annual operating deficit
findings.detail: Service identified as operating at £192k annual net deficit. Proposal is to discontinue the service, eliminating both the deficit and the saving required to offset it. Represents discretionary service review where council is willing to exit non-core activities.
findings.matters: Shows council willing to discontinue services rather than manage deficits. Finance directors watch peer service decisions during budget pressure; lenders track whether councils are pruning non-core activities.
findings.quote: The Duke of Edinburgh Accreditation Service currently operates with an annual net deficit of £192,000. Discontinuing the service would remove this funding requirement and deliver a saving of £192,000 per annum.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C – Savings & Income Generation Proposals
findings.headline: Capita Strategic Services contract ending 30 September 2026, with IT services being brought in-house
findings.detail: £1m saving from CSG contract expiry. Services are being reprocured through a mix of discrete third-party contracts and in-house delivery. IT elements are being insourced rather than continuing the outsourced arrangement, signalling a directional shift from outsourcing.
findings.matters: Major contract transition happening immediately; peers observe how others manage large contract exits. IT insourcing decision represents a shift in service delivery model that other councils evaluating outsourcing deals will monitor. Lenders track major contract transitions as operational change risk.
findings.quote: Services currently provided under the contract have been reprocured through a combination of discreet third party contracts, with some elements of the IT service being brought in-house.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C – Savings & Income Generation Proposals
findings.headline: New Revenues contract projected to save £4.36m over five years, the largest single savings initiative
findings.detail: Replaces existing Revenues function contract with cost reductions phased across the period: £1.7m in 2028/29, £480k in 2029/30, and £2.18m in 2031/32. Reflects contract renegotiation or respecification delivering efficiency gains in a core transactional service.
findings.matters: Largest single-line efficiency saving in the plan, affecting a transactional service common across all councils. Finance directors track peer performance on contract cost reduction. Lenders monitor whether councils are realizing contracted savings.
findings.quote: Reduction in costs of new Revenues contract over the life of the contract

findings.paper_title: Appendix C – Savings & Income Generation Proposals
findings.headline: Greenwich Leisure Ltd contract forecast to deliver £1.2m income above projection in 2028/29
findings.detail: The only positive variance shown across the savings plan. While most contracts are scrutinised for efficiency, GLL is projected to over-deliver against income assumptions. This represents operational performance outperformance on a major council services contract.
findings.matters: Positive variance on major contracts is rare in savings plans; shows active contract management delivering better-than-budgeted performance. Lenders and peer finance directors watch whether councils are extracting value from major outsourced contracts.
findings.quote: Over-delivery against projected income from Greenwich Leisure Ltd (GLL) - the organisation responsible for running leisure centres in Barnet, on the council's behalf

findings.paper_title: Appendix C – Savings & Income Generation Proposals
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation cost control includes occupancy audit pilot to identify non-occupied units and pursue evictions
findings.detail: £2.035m in TA savings span housing options redesign, mediation, occupancy checks, and move-ons from expensive placements. Council is explicitly deploying occupancy audits to identify non-occupancy and sub-letting in both private and in-house stock, with a view to pursuing eviction proceedings to free properties for households in housing need. Pilot data shows 76 percent of outcomes sustained for 14 months.
findings.matters: Shows how council is implementing direct occupancy recovery as a cost control measure. Finance directors across councils dealing with TA growth will watch this approach; lenders track whether councils are managing growing TA exposure through active intervention.
findings.figures: £2,035m total TA savings; 3,036 units in use end May 2026; 76 percent of occupancy-check outcomes sustained for 14 months; 69 percent of TA stock is emergency nightly-paid or block-booked
findings.quote: In these cases, Barnet Homes may be able to pursue eviction proceedings, to free up properties that can be re-let to households who have a pressing housing need.
